Skid marks can be generated when one or more tires loses grip with the racing surface.
The relative volume of your car's engine.
The relative volume of all engines except yours.

The relative volume of all track surface sounds such as tire scrubbing, skidding, and road noise. Scrubbing and skidding provide vital audio feedback, so think twice before reducing this volume level!

To re-assign a control, click to the right of its name. KEYBOARD USERS: By default, the steering, throttle, and brake functions may only be assigned to the numeric keypad. Click the Advanced button if you would rather use different keys.
This number can reduce unwanted oscillations of the wheel that arise due to latency, although too large a number can introduce jerkiness into the force output.
Smooths out the input from your throttle control.  This is useful for digital controls such as game pads and the keys on your keyboard.  Set to 0 for instant response.
Smooths out the input from your braking control.  This is useful for digital controls such as game pads and the keys on your keyboard.  Set to 0 for instant response.

Sets the steering linearity. If you are using a steering wheel, moving the slider toward Linear may give you more precise control. If you are using a joystick to steer, you will probably get better results by moving the slider toward Non-Linear. NOTE: If you are steering with a digital controller such as the keyboard or a standard gamepad, this option will be disabled.

If checked, equips your car with an anti-lock braking system.  While anti-lock brakes make the car easier for the novice driver to control, the experienced driver will be able to brake more efficiently with this option turned off. NOTE: If braking has been assigned to a button or a key rather than a controller axis, this aid will be turned on by default. Otherwise, the car would be very difficult to control while braking.

If checked, equips your car with an automatic clutch. While the manual clutch can provide greater shifting precision, it requires proper heel and toe downshift technique and therefore is recommended only for experienced users. The manual clutch is not available if Automatic Shifting has been selected.

If checked, equips your car with a traction control system. While traction control makes the car easier for the novice driver to control, the experienced driver will be able to accelerate and corner more efficiently with this option turned off. NOTE: If the throttle has been assigned to a button or a key rather than a controller axis, this aid will be turned on be default. Otherwise, the car would be very difficult to control while accelerating.
Choose a control to engage the clutch.
The chassis type used on this car. This can be modified only when a driver is created.
The ability of the car to slip through the air with a minimum of drag. A higher Aero rating means less drag, which translates to more speed.
A high rating translates to quicker times for all pit operations: changing tires, adding fuel, making setup adjustments, and repairing damage.

A measurement of the team's willingness to take pitting risks in order to gain track position. This can be done in several ways, the most obvious of which involves taking none or two tires rather than four. As this value increases, the team becomes more willing to take such chances. Because of this fact, a high Strategy rating isn't necessarily better than a low one.

Multiplies the tire wear and fuel usage rates by the indicated value.  1x translates to normal usage, 2x double, 3x triple, and 4x quadruple usage.  This option is useful for setting up a short race which normally would not require a pit stop.

Arcade mode has fewer rules to follow and features a relatively easy-to-drive car with unrealistically high levels of power and grip. Simulation mode features the full set of NASCAR rules and an ultra-realistic physics model that provides the most authentic NASCAR driving experience available outside of a race car.

The damage level used. In Moderate mode, the car is able to withstand significantly more damage than it can in Realistic mode. Note that even if None is selected, it is still possible to blow the engine and wear the tires to the point of failure.

If checked, there will be a realistic chance of suffering a mechanical failure. Note that even if this option is unchecked, it is still possible to blow the engine and wear the tires to the point of failure.

If checked, a Hardcore Mode can be selected.  If the Visual mode is selected, all competitors will be forced to race from the cockpit view, with smoke and windshield buildup enabled.  If the Driving Aids mode is selected, anti-lock brakes, stability control, steering assistance, and traction control will be disabled for all competitors.

Replay time bar. Clicking on any point of the time bar will move the slider control and cause the replay to jump to the corresponding point in time. More precise control can be achieved by clicking on the slider control, dragging it to the desired point in the replay, and releasing it.
Speed, Gear, Throttle, and Brake data for the selected driver.  Throttle and Brake information is available only for the local player driver.

This affects the ratio of motion between your game controller (the car steering wheel) and the steering of the front tires.  A higher number gives you finer control, a smaller number gives you fast response.

The desired amount of fuel. The car's fuel level is fully adjustable only in Testing mode. In all other game modes, fuel may be added to the tank, but not removed.  At Daytona and Talladega, a 13.5-gallon fuel tank is used.  At all other tracks, a 22-gallon tank is used.

Each tire's temperature is taken in three places: inner edge (I), middle (M), and outer edge (O). Note that the location of the INNER and OUTER edges depends upon the side of the car being examined. Cold pressure is measured when the tire is mounted. Hot, or operating pressure is measured at each pit stop.
Contains the following setup elements: Tire pressure, shock compression and rebound, springs, camber, caster, ride height, front brake bias, front toe-out, sway bars, and track bar.
Contains the following setup elements: Grille tape, spoiler, differential and transmission ratios.
More forward weight increases stability for high-speed cornering and braking. More rear weight permits the car to rotate around slow, sharp corners more quickly.

The qualifying engine gives more power, but will tend to overheat if used for more than a few laps. The race engine is designed to go the full race distance. You are automatically given the qualifying engine in a qualifying session, and the race engine in a happy hour or race session. In practice or testing you are free to try either.

The differential gear ratio is used to adjust all four gears together. A smaller ratio allows for higher top speeds, but produces less torque at the rear wheels, so it will take longer to reach top speed.

A taller gear (smaller number) is better for higher speeds.  A shorter gear (larger number) is better for strong acceleration.  Select gearing such that the car accelerates briskly through gears 1-4, and that the engine RPM tops out around 9,000 (7,000 at the restrictor plate tracks) in top gear.

This is the number of engine revolutions for each revolution of the rear wheels in the given gear. This allows a meaningful comparison of gear ratios when changing both the diff ratio and transmission ratios.
More grille tape reduces drag and increases front downforce, making the car turn better.  More tape also makes the engine run hotter.
A steeper rear spoiler increases drag and rear downforce, making the car tighter.  A flatter spoiler reduces both, and makes the car looser.

Lower tire pressures result in a more forgiving car, and higher tire temperatures. Higher pressures allow higher top speeds with less temperature buildup. The recommended pressure will keep the middle (M) temperature on the tires near the average of the inside (I) and outside (O) temperatures. Going higher than recommended can result in more speed at a high-speed track, but the loss in grip can hurt at slower tracks.

At the RF shock, adding compression (higher number) will tighten the car on corner entry, while less will make it looser.  For the LF, adding compression will loosen the car on corner entry, while less will tighten it.  For the RR, adding compression will loosen the car on corner exit, while less will make it tighter.  For the LR, adding compression will tighten the car on corner exit, while less will make it looser.

At the RF shock, adding rebound (higher number) will loosen the car on corner exit, while less will tighten it.  For the LF, in high-speed corners adding rebound will loosen the car on corner exit, while less will tighten it.  In low-speed corners, the exit effect will be reversed.  For the RR, adding rebound will tighten the car on corner entry, while less will loosen it.  For the LR, adding rebound will loosen the car on corner entry, while less will tighten it.

Increasing RF spring stiffness will tighten the car, particularly on corner entry.  Softening it will have the reverse effect.  Increasing LF can make the car turn better on corner entry, but may tighten it in the remainder of the corner.  Increasing RR will make the car loose, particularly mid-corner and on exit. In high-speed corners, aerodynamic effects may overcome this.  Increasing LR will make the car tighter on corner exit, but may loosen it in mid-corner.
Adding negative camber on a right side tire (or adding positive camber on a left side tire) increases lateral grip on that tire, up to a point.  Excessive camber can greatly increase tire wear.

Adding positive caster 'removes wedge' from the car as the tires are steered, making the car looser.  Unequal caster (caster split) imposes unbalanced forces on the steering system that the driver can feel.
Raising the track bar loosens the car. Increasing the split (running higher right side than left side) loosens the car under power and in high-banked corners, and tightens it under braking.
If the car doesn't turn well under braking, decrease the front brake bias. If it wants to spin under braking, increase the front bias. Go with the lowest front bias you can control.

Roll couple can be thought of as the car's weight bias as it's cornering. Displayed as percentage front. Roll couple is not directly adjustable; its value is derived from your spring and sway bar settings. Increasing roll couple will tighten the car and promote understeer, while decreasing it will loosen it and promote oversteer.
Increasing front toe-out settles the car in a turn, but too much can produce understeer. 1/8 inch toe-out is a very common setting.
